title: Curriculum Is a Localist Model of a Distributed Mind
author: Becky Allen
summary: Allen explains why her six-month attempt to write definitive rules for chunking curriculum into knowledge components kept failing. Drawing on Suri and McClelland's The Emergent Mind and Wittgenstein's problem of defining a game, she argues that knowledge in the brain is distributed rather than stored in discrete units. Dividing a curriculum is therefore a localist projection onto a continuous reality, and designers impose structure through tacit expert judgement rather than discover it. She shows that Koedinger's empirical definition of knowledge components relocates rather than resolves the circularity. Her conclusion is that components are useful fictions, and that the right question is what a given decomposition is for (adaptive platforms, instruction, retrieval, assessment).
points: Knowledge is stored as distributed patterns, so there is no 'dog neuron' and no natural boundary around a piece of knowledge.
Every chunking principle breaks at the margins because each is a different projection of the same distributed space.
Curriculum designers feel they are discovering structure but are imposing it, with tacit expertise filling the gaps.
Koedinger's data-driven knowledge components inherit the structure of the assessment and instruction used to find them.
Treat knowledge components as purpose-built useful fictions and ask what the decomposition is for.
quotes: The book explores how knowledge is stored in the brain — not in tidy, separable units, but as patterns of activation distributed across vast numbers of neurons. There’s no “dog neuron.” Your understanding of dogs is a pattern, one that overlaps with wolves, pets, loyalty, and that terrier you had as a child.

When we divide a curriculum into components — units that can be sequenced, taught, assessed, and revisited — we are acting as localists. We’re projecting a continuous, context-dependent reality onto a grid of discrete categories. The projection can be more or less useful.

When a curriculum designer decomposes a domain into units, it feels like discovering the structure of the knowledge. It isn’t. They’re imposing a structure, using their own distributed understanding to make judgement calls about where to draw boundaries.

This is appealing. But it doesn’t escape the problem; it relocates it. To identify the clusters, you first need assessment items; and deciding what items to write requires the same decomposition decisions you were trying to avoid.

If knowledge in the brain is distributed, then knowledge components are not cognitive primitives waiting to be discovered. They’re modelling constructs or useful fictions created to serve particular systems. And different systems need different fictions.

The right question is never “what are the true units of knowledge?” It’s: useful for what? Once you’re clear about your purpose, the decomposition follows — not from the nature of knowledge, but from the nature of what you’re trying to build.
